ABSTRACT Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively mitigates the knowledge cutoff and hallucination issues of large language models by incorporating external knowledge bases. However, standard RAG applies a uniform retrieval strategy to all question types and feeds redundant retrieval results directly into the generator, leading to high token consumption and potentially degraded answer quality. This paper proposes SAC-RAG (Semantic Adaptive Compress RAG), a unified framework that integrates questiontype-adaptive retrieval with context compression. SAC-RAG first classifies queries into three types—factual, definitional, and reasoning—via an LLM classifier, applies a differentiated retrieval strategy for each type, then uses a unified LLM context compression module to extract evidence snippets, and finally generates answers from the compressed and refined context. To independently quantify the contribution of each component, we design four progressive ablation experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets—HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue—and evaluate using four metrics: Exact Match, F1, Recall@10, and token consumption. Experimental results show that SAC-RAG reduces token consumption by 38%–58% at the cost of only a 1–2 percentage point EM drop, with EM actually improving after compression for reasoning-type questions, achieving the optimal quality–efficiency trade-off in terms of token consumption, with a moderate increase in per-query latency due to additional LLM calls. SAC-RAG offers a modular and interpretable optimization solution for the efficient deployment of RAG in real-world settings. INDEX TERMS Context compression, multi-hop question answering, question-type-adaptive retrieval, retrieval-augmented generation, semantic classification. I. INTRODUCTION Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well across a wide range of natural language processing tasks, yet they suffer from two inherent limitations: knowledge cutoff and factual hallucination. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances LLM responses by retrieving relevant documents from external knowledge bases and has become the dominant approach for addressing these issues. However, standard RAG systems have two critical blind spots. First, they apply a uniform retrieval strategy to all questions, ignoring the fact that different question types require The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Alba Amato . differentiated retrieval approaches. Second, they feed all retrieved document chunks directly into the generator, introducing substantial noise and redundancy [1], which incurs high token consumption and may degrade answer quality. Recent studies further reveal that relevant evidence can still be overlooked within long retrieved contexts, leading to a ‘‘lost-in-retrieval’’ phenomenon [2] that calls for more targeted context handling. Existing work typically optimizes retrieval or compression in isolation. On the retrieval side, Adaptive-RAG [3] dynamically selects a retrieval strategy (no retrieval / singlestep retrieval / multi-step retrieval) based on question complexity, but it does not incorporate a context compression mechanism. On the compression side, methods such as LLMLingua [5] and LongLLMLingua compress retrieved context on top of standard retrieval, effectively reducing token consumption; however, they operate on a fixed retrieval pipeline without considering question-type differences in the retrieval stage. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work unifies question-type-adaptive retrieval and context compression within a single framework. To address these limitations, this paper proposes SAC-RAG (Semantic Adaptive Compress RAG), a unified framework that integrates question-type-adaptive retrieval with context compression. SAC-RAG first classifies each user query into one of three semantic types via an LLM classifier: Fact, Definition, and Reasoning. SAC-RAG employs a differentiated retrieval strategy for each type. Fact-type questions use hybrid retrieval combining BM25 sparse retrieval and Milvus dense vector retrieval with BGE cross-encoder reranking. Definition-type questions adopt pure semantic vector retrieval. Reasoning-type questions are decomposed into multiple sub-questions by an LLM, with results merged after parallel retrieval. Once retrieval is complete, results of all types pass through a unified LLM context compression module to extract evidence snippets, which are then fed into the generator to produce the final answer. To systematically validate the independent contribution of each component, we design four progressive ablation settings on three multi-hop question answering datasets—HotpotQA [6], 2WikiMultiHopQA [7], and MuSiQue [8]—namely Naive RAG (baseline), Compress RAG (compression only), Adaptive RAG (adaptive retrieval only), and SAC-RAG (the full framework). Evaluation covers four metrics: Exact Match (EM), F1, Recall@10, and average token consumption. Experimental results show that: (1) adaptive retrieval is the primary driver of answer quality improvement, boosting EM from 0.560 to 0.611 ( +9.1%) and Recall@10 from 0.787 to 0.880 (+11.8%) on HotpotQA; (2) context compression reduces token consumption by 55–58% with EM decreasing by only 1–2 percentage points; (3) SAC-RAG achieves the optimal quality–efficiency trade-off; on Reasoning-type questions, EM improves after compression (HotpotQA: 0.455→0.577). Unlike previous studies that optimize either retrieval or compression independently, SAC-RAG coordinates semantic-aware retrieval and context compression within a unified framework. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • A question-semantic-type-based adaptive retrieval framework with three differentiated retrieval strategies; • A unified architecture, SAC-RAG, that integrates adaptive retrieval and context compression; • Systematic ablation experiments that independently quantify the contribution of each component, providing clear guidance for RAG system optimization. II. RELATED WORK A. EVOLUTION OF RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was introduced by Lewis et al. [9] in 2020, with the core idea of retrieving relevant documents from external knowledge bases as additional context before an LLM generates an answer, thereby addressing knowledge cutoff and hallucination. Early RAG systems relied on dense vector retrieval [10], mapping queries and documents into a shared vector space for nearest neighbor search. Gao et al. [11] categorized the evolution of RAG into three stages: Naive RAG uses a fixed retrieve-thengenerate pipeline; Advanced RAG introduces pre- and postretrieval optimizations such as query rewriting, reranking, and compression; Modular RAG decomposes the system into independently replaceable functional modules, supporting iterative retrieval and adaptive scheduling. A recent systematic review [12] further confirms this taxonomy through a PRISMA-compliant analysis of 128 highly cited RAG studies, identifying modular and policy-driven architectures as the prevailing trend. Within this framework, training paradigms such as Atlas [13], context-prefix schemes such as In-Context RALM [14], and standardized benchmarks such as BEIR [15] emerged in succession. As retrieved documents grow longer, however, LLMs become less effective at using key information in extended contexts [1]: redundant content not only raises computational cost but also introduces noise that can degrade answer quality. These issues are particularly acute in multi-hop reasoning, where retrieval spans multiple documents of uneven relevance, demanding both precision in retrieval strategies and efficiency in context utilization— as well as coordination between the two. Existing work addressing these bottlenecks falls into three main directions: adaptive retrieval, context compression, and joint optimization of retrieval and reasoning. B. ADAPTIVE RETRIEVAL METHODS Adaptive retrieval adjusts retrieval strategies based on query characteristics to obtain more precise context. For strategy selection, Adaptive-RAG [3] routes questions among no-retrieval, single-step, and multi-step retrieval paths based on question complexity; Self-RAG [16] uses a selfreflection mechanism to trigger retrieval on demand during generation; FLARE [17] actively supplements retrieval based on token confidence during decoding. For retrieval quality, V endi-RAG [18] introduces a diversity metric to balance coverage and relevance of retrieved documents; REPLUG [19] improves reliability through multi-retriever ensembling. On the input side, Ma et al. [20] proposed the Rewrite-Retrieve-Read framework, training a compact rewriting model to optimize queries before retrieval. More recently, LLM-based generation-augmented rewriting methods such as GaQR [21] further leverage chain-of-thought reasoning to expand queries, achieving substantial retrieval recall improvements. A parallel line of work explores query routing at the model level. RouteLLM [22] learns query-aware routing policies that balance response quality VOLUME 14, 2026 117407

However, these routing methods primarily address model selection or query-complexity-based dispatch, whereas SAC-RAG adapts retrieval strategies within a unified pipeline according to semantic question types—a distinction that yields finergrained control over the retrieval process. A shared limitation of these methods is that their adaptation axis centers on question complexity or token confidence, without designing differentiated retrieval mechanisms based on question semantic type (factual, definitional, reasoning). As a result, retrieval strategies lack a structured understanding of the nature of the question. C. CONTEXT COMPRESSION METHODS Context compression aims to reduce redundancy in retrieval results, lowering token consumption during generation. LLMLingua [5] introduced selective compression of retrieval results using a small language model; LongLLMLingua [24] extended this to long-context settings. In terms of compression strategy, RECOMP [25] formalized compression as a summarization task; BRIEF [26] introduced a queryaware mechanism that doubles the compression rate while maintaining answer quality; LLMLingua-2 [27] proposed a task-agnostic data distillation approach. SARA [28] further combines fine-grained textual spans with compact semantic compression vectors to improve context efficiency under strict token budgets. The growing focus on token efficiency has also motivated agentic frameworks such as TeaRAG[29], which jointly compresses retrieved content and reasoning chains to achieve significant token reduction while preserving accuracy. A common limitation of these methods is that compression operates on top of a fixed retrieval strategy: the retrieval stage is unaware of downstream compression needs, and the compression stage does not exploit type information from the retrieval stage. The two components remain independent, lacking co-design. D. JOINT RETRIEVAL AND REASONING In multi-hop QA, retrieval and reasoning are not independent stages—reasoning requires multiple retrieval steps to supply intermediate evidence, and retrieval strategies shift dynamically with each reasoning step. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [30] established the approach of improving reasoning through intermediate steps; ReAct [31] interleaves reasoning and action, deciding after each reasoning step whether new retrieval is needed; IRCoT [32] embeds retrieval within each step of the CoT reasoning chain. For task decomposition, DecomP [33] and DSP [34] adopt a decompose-retrieve-merge strategy; ChainRAG [2] addresses the information loss problem in sub-question decomposition through progressive retrieval-and-rewriting over a sentence graph. KiRAG[4] further incorporates knowledge triples into iterative retrieval, bridging information gaps across reasoning steps. These works show the value of jointly optimizing retrieval and reasoning. However, they focus on retrieval–reasoning synergy, while the joint optimization of retrieval and compression remains an open problem: no existing method unifies adaptive retrieval and context compression within a single framework. E. RESEARCH GAP AND MOTIVATION The analysis of the three directions above reveals a shared limitation: the components of a RAG system— retrieval, compression, and reasoning—are still optimized as independent modules. Adaptive retrieval addresses how to retrieve, but does not consider how the retrieval results will be compressed; context compression addresses how to condense, but does not exploit type information from the retrieval stage to guide compression strategy; joint retrieval and reasoning demonstrates the value of co-design, but this principle has yet to be extended to retrieval and compression. The core motivation of SAC-RAG is to fill this gap: to build a unified framework in which question-type-adaptive retrieval and context compression work together. In SAC-RAG, the classifier’s output determines the retrieval strategy; the resulting type-specific retrieval outputs naturally differ in document count, redundancy, and information density, which shapes the input to the downstream compression module. Although compression itself uses a unified prompt and logic across all question types, the diversity of its inputs produces type-adaptive compression effects. This indirect coordination through the data flow distinguishes SAC-RAG from prior modular designs where retrieval and compression operate as independently configurable modules. Retrieval strategies are differentiated by semantic type, compression processes diverse retrieval outputs with a consistent logic, and the two components achieve positive complementarity in the quality–efficiency trade-off. III. METHOD A. SAC-RAG SYSTEM OVERVIEW The SAC-RAG pipeline, as shown in Figure1, consists of five core stages: question classification, type-specific retrieval, context compression, answer generation, and evaluation. Given a user query q, the system first determines its semantic type t via a question classifier, then selects the corresponding retrieval strategy to retrieve a document set from the knowledge base D, after which a unified context compression module extracts refined evidence snippets, and the system finally generates the answer ˆa. B. QUESTION CLASSIFIER The question classifier uses an LLM with a structured prompt and few-shot examples to categorize queries into three types. C. TYPE-SPECIFIC RETRIEVAL STRATEGIES 1) FACT: HYBRID RETRIEVAL + RERANKING Fact-type questions involve specific entities and keywords. Relying solely on dense vector retrieval may miss exact term matches due to semantic generalization. SAC-RAG adopts a hybrid retrieval strategy, where the combined score for a candidate document d is defined as follows: SFact(q, d)=λ· BM25(q, d)+ (1−λ)· cos(eq, ed ) (2) where eq and ed are dense vectors of the query and document encoded by text-embedding-3-small, and the BM25 term matching score is computed as: BM25(q, d)= ∑ w∈q IDF(w)· f (w, d)(k1+ 1) f (w, d)+ k1(1− b+ b |d| avgdl ) (3) where f (w, d) is the term frequency of w in document d,|d| is the document length, avgdl is the average document length, and k1 and b are BM25 hyperparameters (default k1= 1.5, b= 0.75). The specific procedure is: 1) BM25 sparse retrieval: based on spaCy tokenization and rank_bm25.BM25Okapi, retrieving top-10 by term matching. 2) Dense vector retrieval: ANN retrieval via Milvus using Cosine similarity, retrieving top-10. 3) Merge and deduplication: the two result sets are merged and deduplicated by doc_id. 4) BGE reranking: using the bge-reranker-base crossencoder to score each candidate and selecting the top-10. 2) DEFINITION: PURE SEMANTIC RETRIEVAL Definition-type questions focus on the meaning of a single concept, where semantic vector similarity is sufficient to cover the relevant content. For definition-type questions, SAC-RAG uses only Milvus dense vector retrieval (Cosine similarity), taking the top-8 documents directly into the subsequent compression and generation stages, avoiding unnecessary hybrid retrieval overhead. 3) REASONING: SUB-QUESTION DECOMPOSITION + PARALLEL RETRIEVAL Reasoning-type questions require support from multiple knowledge points, and a single retrieval query may fail to cover all reasoning paths. CONTEXT COMPRESSION The top-k documents produced during the retrieval stage are fed into a unified LLM compression module, which extracts evidence snippets relevant to the question through a custom prompt: Ct= Compress(q, Rt ), t∈{Fact, Definition, Reasoning} (5) The compression uses a unified prompt and compression logic for all question types, but the input retrieved document set Rt varies by question type (differing in k value and retrieval strategy). E. ANSWER GENERATION The compressed context Ct is merged with the original query q and fed into the LLM to generate the final answer ˆa. All experimental groups use the same LLM configuration to ensure fair comparison. IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP A. DATASETS AND EVALUATION METRICS Experiments are conducted on three English multi-hop opendomain question answering datasets. Dataset statistics and evaluation metrics are shown in Table 1. The four evaluation metrics follow standard practices in the retrieval-augmented generation literature: EM and F1 follow the answer quality evaluation approach established by DPR [10], Recall@10 assesses retrieval quality, and average token consumption (Avg Tokens) follows the efficiency metric introduced by LLMLingua [5]. All answer quality metrics are computed after applying normalize_answer() normalization (Unicode NFKD, lowercasing, punctuation and article removal, whitespace collapsing). The formal definitions of Recall@K and F1 are as follows: Recall@K=|DK ret∩ DGT| |DGT| (6) F1= 2·|tok(ˆa)∩ tok(a)| |tok(ˆa)|+|tok(a)| (7) where DK ret denotes the set of top-K retrieved documents, DGT denotes the set of ground-truth supporting documents, ˆa and a denote the predicted and ground-truth answers respectively, and tok(·) denotes the normalized token set. B. EXPERIMENTAL ENVIRONMENT The vector database uses Milvus (Collection en_doc_ chunk, 1536 dimensions, Cosine similarity), and metadata storage uses MongoDB. BM25 sparse retrieval is based on rank_bm25.BM25Okapi with spaCy tokenization. The reranker uses BGE bge-reranker-base [35]. For each dataset, 1,000 questions are independently run under 4 RAG configurations, with temperature set to 0 to ensure deterministic outputs. V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS A. OVERALL PERFORMANCE To position SAC-RAG within the RAG research landscape, we first conduct a horizontal comparison with recent representative RAG methods, including standard retrievalaugmented generation (V anilla RAG), iterative retrieval augmentation (IterDRAG [36]), search-augmented retrieval (ReSearch [36]), and Monte Carlo tree search-based autonomous reasoning (AirRAG [36]). These methods use different backbone LLMs and implementation settings; thus this comparison aims to evaluate overall system-level effectiveness rather than serve as a strictly controlled variable experiment.1 As shown in Table 2, two clear patterns emerge. The baselines use different backbone LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B) and implementation settings than SAC-RAG (gpt-5-mini); therefore, this comparison evaluates overall system-level effectiveness rather than isolating framework-specific contributions. The controlled variable ablation study (Table 5) provides the internally consistent comparison. First, SAC-RAG achieves F1 scores comparable to the best-performing methods on HotpotQA and 2Wiki (74.0 vs. 74.9; 66.4 vs. 65.7), and leads significantly on MuSiQue (40.3 vs. 30.3), suggesting that question-type-adaptive retrieval offers greater advantages when retrieval difficulty is high. Second, SAC-RAG is the only method that simultaneously reports token consumption and Recall@10—average tokens of only 1,087–1,918 (vs. 2,407–3,111 for Adaptive RAG, see Table 5), with 1N/R = Not Reported. ABLATION STUDY: DESIGN AND VERIFICATION 1) EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN To independently quantify the contribution of each component, we design four progressive ablation study groups. The configuration and retrieval parameters of each group are shown in Table 4. Using Naïve RAG as the baseline, the remaining three groups incrementally build upon it: Compress RAG adds only the context compression module on top of Naïve RAG’s retrieval results, to independently quantify the contribution of compression; Adaptive RAG adds only the question classifier and type-specific retrieval strategies, to independently quantify the contribution of adaptive retrieval; SAC-RAG, as the full framework, enables both modules simultaneously, to verify their synergistic effect. To visualize the token consumption patterns more directly, Figure 4 presents the per-query average token consumption of the four configurations across the three datasets. SAC-RAG maintains the lowest token consumption among all configurations on all datasets, while Adaptive RAG—despite achieving the best answer quality—incurs substantially higher token overhead than even the Naïve baseline. Compress RAG alone yields noticeable reductions, confirming that the compression module is the primary driver of token savings. D. ANAL YSIS OF COMPRESSION EFFECTS BY QUESTION TYPE The ablation results above validate the overall effectiveness of adaptive retrieval and context compression. However, a deeper question constitutes the theoretical premise of SAC-RAG’s design—does context compression affect different question types uniformly? If compression effects were type-independent, there would be no need for differentiated retrieval after classification; conversely, if different types respond to compression in significantly different ways, this validates the design rationale of ‘‘classify first, then retrieve’’ in SAC-RAG. To answer this question, Table 6 presents the percategory performance of Adaptive RAG and SAC-RAG across different question types. Reasoning questions represent the category where compression is most effective. On HotpotQA, SAC-RAG achieves an EM of 0.577 on Reasoning questions, a 26.8% improvement over Adaptive RAG’s 0.455. On 2Wiki, Adaptive RAG’s EM on Reasoning questions is as high as 0.859, while SAC-RAG achieves 0.855, essentially on par, with token consumption dropping from 3,255 to 1,490 (−54.2%). For questions involving multi-step reasoning chains, compression effectively filters out noise in the retrieved results, allowing the LLM to focus on critical evidence. On MuSiQue, the Reasoning EM decreases modestly from 0.253 to 0.220 (−3.3 pp), suggesting that when retrieval quality is already low (Recall@10=0.372–0.385), the compressed context may lose critical evidence fragments that are too sparse to survive filtering. Factual questions constitute the largest category by count. On both datasets, SAC-RAG’s EM on Fact questions decreases by 2.4% (HotpotQA: 0.614→0.599) and 4.9% (2Wiki: 0.528→0.502), respectively, compared to Adaptive RAG. Given the 55–60% reduction in token consumption, this trade-off is acceptable in practical applications. Definition questions have the smallest sample size (HotpotQA 20 instances, 2Wiki 5 instances). These sample sizes reflect the natural distribution of definitional queries in the original datasets, and the resulting per-category metrics should be interpreted with appropriate caution. On 2Wiki, SAC-RAG EM reaches 1.000 (5/5), outperforming Adaptive RAG’s 0.800; on HotpotQA, EM drops from 0.650 to 0.450. A detailed analysis is provided in Section VI. Synthesizing the per-type results across all three categories, Reasoning questions exhibit the most favorable compression trade-off (EM improves or stays level with large token savings on two of three datasets), Fact questions show slight degradation, and Definition questions are highly sensitive—the response patterns to compression differ markedly by question type. This finding confirms the necessity of type-differentiated retrieval strategies and supports the future design of type-adaptive compression strategies (see Section VI-C). E. QUALITY-EFFICIENCY PARETO ANAL YSIS Figure 5 illustrates the trade-off between retrieval quality (Recall@10) and token consumption for the four experimental configurations across three datasets. SAC-RAG lies on the Pareto frontier on all datasets, achieving Recall@10 nearly on par with Adaptive RAG at the lowest token consumption. Compress RAG has low token usage but insufficient retrieval quality, while Naïve RAG underperforms on both dimensions. F. TIME EFFICIENCY Naïve RAG is the fastest (HotpotQA ∼9.6 s/instance), Adaptive RAG adds classification and differentiated retrieval overhead (∼21.5 s), and SAC-RAG further adds a compression step (∼27.8 s). These additional LLM calls (classifier, sub-question decomposer, compressor) dominate the time overhead. Since the computational cost arises from API calls rather than local GPU computation, GPU memory and FLOPs are not directly comparable; per-query latency is reported as the primary efficiency metric. See Section VI-C for further discussion. VI. DISCUSSION A. OVERALL PERFORMANCE OF SAC-RAG The consistent performance of SAC-RAG across three multi-hop QA datasets validates the effectiveness of combining question-type-adaptive retrieval with context compression. Adaptive RAG achieves the best answer quality on all datasets, with EM scores of 0.611, 0.595, and 0.284 on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue, respectively. ERROR ANAL YSIS OF COMPRESSION DEGRADATION To understand under what circumstances context compression leads to degraded answer quality, we conduct a fine-grained degradation analysis on the HotpotQA dataset. Comparing the per-question F1 scores of Adaptive RAG and SAC-RAG, the results are shown in Table 7. Definition-type questions are the most sensitive to compression. By comparing the retrieved documents before and after compression for the same question, we find that the top-8 retrieved documents are identical, ruling out retrieval differences as the cause of degradation and confirming that the issue lies in the post-compression answer generation stage. A representative case: Question: ‘‘Who is this American cartoonist, writer, producer, animator, and voice actor that worked with this multiple Shuster Award, Harvey Award and Eisner Award nominee and an Eisner Award–winning comic book creator?’’ Ground truth: Matt Groening Adaptive RAG: Matt Groening ✓ SAC-RAG: Steve Purcell ✗ The retrieval context simultaneously contains relevant documents about both Matt Groening and Steve Purcell. In the full context, the LLM correctly identifies the target person; however, in the compressed and refined context, the distinguishing cues between the two entities are weakened. This case reveals the core risk of compression for definitiontype questions: when multiple entities of the same type co-occur in the context, compression may weaken the distinguishing cues between them. Fact-type questions show a slight but systematic drop. Among 958 Fact questions, 63 (6.6%) show F1 drops. The typical degradation pattern is the loss of key factual details during compression. For instance, the question ‘‘Where was the place of death of Vigrahapala I (Pala Dynasty)’s father?’’ has the ground-truth answer Peshawar; Adaptive RAG answers correctly, while SAC-RAG incorrectly answers Bengal. Reasoning-type questions benefit from compression. Among the 22 Reasoning questions in HotpotQA, only 1 shows degradation, and SAC-RAG’s EM on the Reasoning category improves from 0.455 to 0.577 (+26.8%). Compression filters out noisy documents in the reasoning path, allowing the LLM to focus on core evidence fragments. C. LIMITATIONS (1) Limited classifier granularity. The answer generation and context compression in this study rely on gpt-5-mini and qwen-flash, respectively; different LLMs may exhibit different generation capabilities and compression behaviors. However, internal validity is ensured through controlled variable comparisons under the same LLM configuration. (4) Single-run evaluation. All experiments were conducted under deterministic decoding (temperature= 0) to minimize generation variance. Future work should include repeated trials to further quantify pipelinelevel variance introduced by the retriever, classifier, and compression modules. (5) Dataset coverage. Current experiments are conducted on three English multi-hop QA datasets. Generalization performance on non-English datasets and vertical domain datasets remains to be verified. (6) Classifier error propagation. Despite the satisfactory standalone performance of the classifier (92.0% accuracy), misclassification may still propagate to downstream retrieval strategy selection, compression, and generation stages. The impact of classifier errors on end-to-end performance warrants further investigation. D. FUTURE WORK (1) Type-adaptive compression strategies. (2) Classification system expansion. CONCLUSION This paper proposes SAC-RAG, a unified framework that integrates question-type-adaptive retrieval with context compression. SAC-RAG uses an LLM classifier to categorize queries in real time into factual, definitional, and reasoning types, and employs differentiated retrieval strategies for each type—Fact-type questions use hybrid BM25 and dense vector retrieval with reranking, Definition-type questions adopt pure semantic retrieval, and Reasoning-type questions undergo sub-question decomposition followed by parallel retrieval— after which all retrieval results pass through a unified LLM context compression module to extract evidence snippets before generating the final answer. Results from four progressive ablation experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue demonstrate that: (1) adaptive retrieval is the primary driver of answer quality improvement, boosting EM by 3.3–5.1 percentage points and Recall@10 by 2.5–9.3 percentage points; (2) context compression reduces token consumption by 38–58% with EM decreasing by only 1–2 percentage points; (3) SAC-RAG achieves the optimal quality–efficiency tradeoff, lying on the Pareto frontier on all three datasets; for reasoning-type questions, compression improves answer quality by filtering out noise. The time overhead (approximately 27.8 s vs. 9.6 s per instance for Naïve RAG on HotpotQA) primarily stems from the additional LLM calls for classification, subquestion decomposition, and compression. This trade-off between token efficiency and latency should be weighed against application-specific deployability requirements. The success of SAC-RAG confirms that optimizing retrieval by question type before applying uniform compression provides a practical solution for reducing LLM API costs in real-world deployments while maintaining answer quality.
